Source: /home/workspace/.claude/skills/jev-code-score/scripts/rubrics.json. Keep in sync by hand; do not fork the wording.
_meta.scale: Every question is a Jev `score`. Levels run 0 (worst) to 4 (best). Higher always means healthier code, so the overall score is a plain mean.

code_smells.instructions: Rate this source code for Martin Fowler-style code smells such as long methods, large classes, feature envy, primitive obsession, data clumps, and shotgun surgery. Higher means fewer, less harmful smells.
criteria: Riddled with smells: bloated methods and classes, feature envy, primitive obsession, and shotgun surgery throughout
Frequent smells that clearly hurt readability and make change unsafe
Some smells present but localized and low impact
Mostly clean; only minor, defensible smells remain
No meaningful code smells; cohesive and well factored

security.instructions: Rate this source code for security by EXPLOITABILITY, not by pattern-matching a checklist. For every candidate issue, ask: is there a concrete input an attacker or untrusted caller could supply that reaches a dangerous sink and causes real harm (auth bypass, code/command execution, cross-tenant data access, secret exposure, traversal outside an intended directory)? Weight heavily anything with a reachable, attacker-influenced path to a dangerous sink — including auth/access checks that fail OPEN (an error, missing token, or unknown case treated as authorized), command injection (untrusted data interpolated or spread into subprocess args or a shell:true call), path traversal (an unsanitized or unvalidated id/name joined into a filesystem path), unsafe deserialization, hardcoded secrets, and injection (SQL/NoSQL/template). Weight lightly, and do not conflate with the above, hardening nits with no plausible attack path: a validated/internal/numeric id used in a path, environment variables passed into a trusted subprocess with no attacker-controlled content, or a missing redundant defense-in-depth layer where the primary control already holds. Confidence calibration: report high confidence (>=0.6) ONLY when you can name the concrete attacker-controlled input and the dangerous sink it reaches; if the exploit path is speculative, framework-mediated, or you cannot tell whether the input is attacker-controlled, keep confidence below 0.6 so the finding routes to human sign-off rather than auto-blocking. Do NOT lower the score for framework-mediated safety that is clearly in force: parameterized or ORM-built queries, inputs already validated or type-narrowed at a trust boundary, auth/escaping middleware that is actually applied on the reachable path, and code reachable only by trusted internal callers with no untrusted entry point. Higher means safer against real, reachable attacks.
criteria: A reachable, exploitable critical vulnerability is present: e.g. authentication or access control that fails open, command injection via unsanitized subprocess arguments, or path traversal from an unsanitized id/name joined into a filesystem path
A serious weakness is present and plausibly reachable by an untrusted caller, even if exploitation needs specific conditions
A real but harder-to-reach concern, or a risky pattern whose exploitability is genuinely unclear and needs human review

Only defense-in-depth nits remain: patterns that look risky in isolation (e.g. env vars passed to a trusted subprocess, an id used in a path) but have no plausible attack path because the value is validated, internal, or not attacker-controlled
No apparent security issues; attacker-reachable input is validated or sanitized before use, auth fails closed, no secrets, safe APIs used

complexity_clean_code.instructions: Rate this source code for complexity and Robert C. Martin clean-code qualities: function size and single responsibility, nesting depth, cyclomatic complexity, and name clarity. Higher means simpler and cleaner.
criteria: Very hard to follow: deep nesting, huge functions, unclear names, high cyclomatic complexity
Often complex or poorly named; frequent cognitive overload
Moderate complexity; several functions or names could be simpler
Mostly simple and well named; small focused functions
Clean and simple: small single-purpose functions, clear names, low complexity

comments.instructions: Rate the comment discipline of this source code. Good comments explain non-obvious why (hidden invariants, external constraints, justified lint or type suppressions, public API doc contracts). Bad comments narrate what the code already says, add banners, leave commented-out code, or preach about workarounds instead of fixing them. Higher means better discipline.
criteria: Pervasive narration, banners, commented-out code, or unjustified lint or type suppressions
Many comments restate the code or justify workarounds rather than fixing them
Mixed: some useful comments alongside several redundant what-comments
Mostly disciplined; only a rare redundant comment
Exemplary: comments explain only non-obvious why; no narration, no dead code, suppressions justified

testability.instructions: Rate how easily this source code can be unit tested: presence of seams, dependency injection, pure versus side-effecting logic, and avoidance of hidden global state. Higher means easier to test. First judge the file's role from its path, the state's `role_hint` (if present), and its content: testability is a category error for a fixture, mock/stub, type declaration, or story file — there is no logic to unit test, so score it near the top by default unless it does something that would genuinely make it awkward to use from a test (e.g. a hidden side effect on import). For a test file itself, judge only whether its own helpers/setup are testable, not whether the test needs testing. Apply the full bar only to application/business logic.
criteria: Untestable: hidden dependencies, global state, side effects fused with logic
Hard to test; would need heavy mocking or refactoring first
Testable with some effort; a few seams missing
Mostly testable; clear seams and injectable dependencies
Highly testable: pure functions, injected dependencies, clean seams — or a non-logic file (fixture/mock/type/story) with nothing that would resist being used in a test

duplication.instructions: Rate this source code for duplication (the DRY principle): repeated logic or structure that should be factored into shared abstractions. Higher means less duplication.
criteria: Extensive copy-paste; the same logic repeated in many places
Frequent duplication that should be factored out
Some repetition; a few blocks worth extracting
Only minor, acceptable repetition
No meaningful duplication; shared logic is well factored

error_handling.instructions: Rate this source code for error handling: validation at boundaries, meaningful error propagation, and absence of swallowed or ignored failures. Higher means more robust. First judge the file's role from its path, the state's `role_hint` (if present), and its content: a fixture, mock/stub, type declaration, story, or test file has no boundary to validate and no failure path of its own, so score it near the top by default rather than penalizing it for lacking try/catch or input validation it was never meant to have. Apply the full bar only to code that actually receives external or caller input — application/business logic, request handlers, parsers, and the like.
criteria: Failure paths ignored or swallowed; no boundary validation; crashes on bad input
Weak: broad catches, silent failures, little validation
Partial: some paths handled but gaps remain at boundaries
Mostly robust; only minor gaps
Robust: validates at boundaries, propagates meaningful errors, no swallowed exceptions — or a non-logic file (fixture/mock/type/story/test) with no boundary of its own to guard
